To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The brain of the bowfin, a primitive actinopterygian fish, is able to control the pH of its tissue fluid by means of an active transport system that can be damaged by mechanical disruption of the ventral glial footplate layer.

the brain of the bowfin, Amia calva, has an active acid-base regulation that is impaired in vitro when the layer of glia footplates at the medullary ventral surface is damaged, and that the tissue's capacity to maintain a stable pH during exposure to acidic or basic incubation fluids is impaired when the footplates are damaged.

1) Bowfin brain tissue can be incubated in vitro for up to 1 h with little damage to the tissue, 2) Bowfin brain can regulate its tissue pH over a range of external pH values, and 3) the glial footplates of bowfin brain are involved in this regulation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the control of pH in the brain of the bowfin.
the mechanisms of hydrogen ion transport and the regulation of tissue pH in the brains of a primitive teleost, the bowfin ( Amia calva ).
the mechanisms of pH regulation in the brain and spinal cord.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the bowfin brain has the capacity for active acid-base control and for hydrogen ion transfer across cell membranes, that this capacity is impaired by damage to the glial footplate layer, and that the capacity is not demonstrable in vitro after 30 min of exposure to artificial CSF.
the pH of the brain is controlled by a combination of intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms.
the brain of the bowfin is capable of controlling its pH in vitro by an active transport of hydrogen ions across its cell membranes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the bowfin brain, as a whole, has a capacity to regulate its pH by active transport of hydrogen ions.
the bowfin's brain is capable of controlling its pH by regulating hydrogen ion transfer, but that the glial footplates play an important part in that regulation.
the brain of the bowfin is capable of active control of its internal pH and that the glial footplate layer is a major component of this regulatory system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the bowfin brain can regulate the pH of its tissue fluids, and that this regulation is mediated in part by a layer of glial cells.
the bowfin brain can regulate its pH, even in vitro, and the glial layer at the ventral medulla oblongate is important for the regulation.
the bowfin is a useful model for studying the mechanisms that regulate pH in fish brain.
